To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the dose distributions of proton beams can be flattened over areas as large as 30 cm in the plane perpendicular to the beam, and that the beam can be delivered with a uniform dose over areas of this size at a source-to-skin (or source-to-object) distance as large as 5 m.

we have developed a method of flattening charged particle dose distributions over a large area, and that we have used this method to flatten the dose distributions of 160-MeV protons over a 30-cm diameter field.

the use of a large SSD (4.6 m) in combination with multiple scattering in a patient and in a scattering medium (water) in the treatment room, results in a beam with very little divergence throughout the treatment volume, and that a combination of blocking and rescattering of the central peak can be used to flatten the dose distribution over large areas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a system for the treatment of cancer by protons.
the development and application of charged-particle beams for radiation therapy.
the development of a proton therapy unit for the treatment of tumors in which a high dose can be delivered to the target with a minimum of damage to normal tissues.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proton radiotherapy program at Harvard is now in a stage of active and successful clinical application.
proton therapy is an effective treatment for certain types of cancer, and that the results are better than those obtained with x-ray therapy.
the Harvard system of charged-particle radiotherapy has been developed to a stage of practical usefulness for the treatment of localized tumors in the head and neck.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a 4-m SSD is required to flatten the dose distribution over 25 cm.
the proton dose distribution can be flattened over large fields with a minimum loss of beam energy, and that the resulting beam is suitable for large-field radiotherapeutic applications.
the dose distributions can be flattened to within 3% over 30-cm diameters and 5% over 45-cm diameters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a 2-mm spot size can be used for the entire treatment volume.
the proton dose distribution can be flattened to a uniform dose within 5% over large areas, and this flattening can be done in a manner which is independent of the patient's size and location.
it is feasible to obtain a large-area, flat dose distribution with a proton beam, and that this can be achieved without the need for an isocentric treatment machine.
